summary: This standards-track document defines the PPP Bandwidth Allocation Protocol and its control protocol, which manage adding and removing links in a PPP multilink bundle as bandwidth needs change.

plainLanguage.summary: When traffic gets heavy, you open extra checkout lanes, and close them when it is quiet.

questions: how do modems add extra phone lines automatically
how does ppp multilink manage bandwidth
when should i add or drop a ppp link
subtitle: Protocols for dynamically adding and removing links in multilink PPP connections.

tldr.problem: When using multilink PPP (multiple phone lines or channels bundled together), there is no standard way to dynamically add extra links when traffic increases or drop them when traffic is light.
tldr.mechanism: BAP and BACP define a negotiation protocol: BACP sets up shared rules between the two peers, and BAP lets either side request to add a new link, have the other side originate a new link, or negotiate dropping a link based on traffic or resource conditions.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can automatically adapt bandwidth to match real-time demand, adding links during busy periods and releasing resources when traffic drops.

today: RFC 2125 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defined a widely-adopted standard for bandwidth-on-demand over multilink PPP. Most modern ISDN terminal adapters and modems that support multilink use BAP for dynamic bandwidth management.

sections.title: The Need for Bandwidth on Demand
sections.content:
PPP multilink lets you bundle multiple phone lines or ISDN channels into a single connection, combining their bandwidth. However, opening and closing extra lines has always been a manual operation or required custom, non-standard protocols.

RFC 2125 defines two complementary protocols: the Bandwidth Allocation Control Protocol (BACP), which is a control channel similar to LCP, and the Bandwidth Allocation Protocol (BAP), which carries the actual messages to add, drop or query links. Together they let both endpoints automatically adjust bandwidth based on traffic conditions or available resources.
sections.plainLanguage: In the old days, you had to manually dial extra lines. Now the modem can do it automatically when it sees the traffic getting heavy.

sections.title: How BAP and BACP Work Together
sections.content:
BACP is a configuration protocol that runs during the PPP connection setup. The two peers negotiate a Favored-Peer option containing a magic number; the peer with the lowest number is the favored peer and breaks ties if both sides send conflicting requests at the same time.

After BACP reaches its opened state, BAP takes over. BAP is sent in special PPP frames (protocol type 0xc02d) and carries eight types of messages: Call-Request, Call-Response, Callback-Request, Callback-Response, Link-Drop-Query-Request, Link-Drop-Query-Response, Call-Status-Indication and Call-Status-Response.

Every BAP request or indication requires a response; if no response arrives, the sender retransmits with the same identifier until it succeeds or gives up.
sections.plainLanguage: BACP is like two managers agreeing on who makes decisions when they disagree. BAP is the actual messages they send each other to say 'open a new line' or 'close this line'.

sections.title: Adding and Dropping Links
sections.content:
To add a link, the requesting peer sends a Call-Request with the desired link type (ISDN, X.25, analog, switched digital, etc.) and link speed in kilobits per second. The other peer responds with Call-Response; if it accepts, the response includes a Phone-Delta option with the phone number to dial. Alternatively, a peer can send Callback-Request to ask the other side to originate the new link.

After attempting to add a link, the originating peer sends Call-Status-Indication to report success or failure. Possible failure codes map to Q.931 causes (the ISDN call control standard), like 'user busy' or 'unassigned number'.

To drop a link, a peer sends Link-Drop-Query-Request naming the link by its Link Discriminator (a unique number assigned during initial LCP negotiation on that link). The other peer responds Request-Ack to agree, Request-Nak to refuse temporarily, or Request-Full-Nak to refuse permanently because it has reached minimum bandwidth. If agreement is reached, the requesting peer then sends an LCP Terminate-Request to actually tear down the link.
sections.plainLanguage: To add a line, you ask the other end what number to call, make the call, and report back if it worked. To drop a line, you ask first, and if they agree, you hang up.

sections.title: BAP Packet Structure and Options
sections.content:
A BAP packet starts with a Type octet (1 through 8 for the eight message types), an Identifier to match requests with responses, and a Length field. Response packets include a Response Code octet: Request-Ack (success), Request-Nak (try again later), Request-Rej (not implemented) or Request-Full-Nak (at bandwidth limit).

The data portion carries options. The Link-Type option specifies the kind of link desired (ISDN, analog, etc.) and its speed in kilobits per second. The Phone-Delta option carries a base phone number and the count of rightmost digits that differ from the original link's number, minimizing the data sent. The No-Phone-Number-Needed option indicates the sender is already configured with the target number. The Reason option is free-form text for logging. The Link-Discriminator option identifies which link to drop. The Call-Status option reports the success or failure of a link addition attempt and whether the endpoint will retry.
sections.plainLanguage: A BAP message is like a postcard: it has a type (what you're asking), a sequence number (so replies match requests), and optional notes about link speed, phone numbers, and why you're asking.

sections.title: Bandwidth Decision-Making
sections.content:
Either peer may monitor traffic to decide when to add or drop links. A peer can monitor only outgoing traffic, both directions, or neither. If both ends monitor bidirectionally, they can co-operate even with a client that does no monitoring.

BAP does not dictate an algorithm for when to add or drop links. Decisions may be based on current link utilization, queue depth, packet loss, latency, or the need to free resources (like a B-channel) for other uses, such as an incoming voice call.

The Link-Drop-Query handshake ensures a link stays open as long as either end determines it is needed. Each peer's response to Link-Drop-Query-Request is based on its own monitoring; the link is dropped only if both agree. If one peer wants to force a drop without negotiation (for example, to answer an incoming call), it simply sends an LCP Terminate-Request without asking.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side can watch the traffic and decide if more lines are needed. They ask each other before closing a line, so if one side is still busy, the line stays open.

sections.title: Resolving Simultaneous Requests
sections.content:
A race condition occurs when both peers send Call-Request, Callback-Request or Link-Drop-Query-Request at the same time. To break the tie, both sides use the Favored-Peer magic number negotiated during BACP setup. The peer whose magic number is lower is favored and its request takes precedence.

The magic number is typically 1 for the initiator of the connection and 0xFFFFFFFF for the responder, but must be random if it is unclear which side initiated (for example on a leased line). A magic number of zero is illegal and must be rejected with Configure-Nak.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sides send a message at the same time, they flip a coin beforehand: the one with the lower magic number wins.

sections.title: Link Discriminators
sections.content:
Each link in a multilink bundle is assigned a unique Link Discriminator during the initial LCP negotiation on that link. This is a 2-octet identifier that allows BAP messages to refer to a specific link without ambiguity. Each peer assigns its own discriminators independently, so a link may have two different discriminator values depending on which end you are on.

When BAP needs to identify a link (especially in Link-Drop-Query messages), it includes the discriminator that the peer sent in its LCP Configure-Request. This lets the receiver know exactly which link the message is about.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line gets a ticket number so that when you say 'drop this line', everyone knows which one you mean.
